newsitem.title: RUSSIA: CIS premiers approve integration guidelines.
newsitem.headline: CIS premiers approve integration guidelines.

text.p: Prime ministers from 12 former Soviet republics met in Moscow on Friday, five years after the creation of their loose Commonwealth, to chart a course for economic integration.
But some Moscow officials insisted that close cooperation between members of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) should not be reached at Russia's expense.
"We have done much in developing the integration of our states," Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told a news conference after the meeting.
"But we cannot be fully happy with the results."
Eight premiers signed the draft guidelines which will be considered at a summit of CIS leaders due in late January.
But the prime ministers of Uzbekistan, Georgia, Azerbaijan, and Turkmenistan decided not to back the draft.

Kremlin officials have said they assume the summit will go ahead, despite Russian President Boris Yeltsin's latest illness. Yeltsin, who had open heart surgery last November, has been in hospital for over a week with pneumonia.
Doctors say that the Russian leader, who turns 66 on February 1, is feeling better, but they have not said when he can leave hospital or return to work.
The CIS, now grouping all the former Soviet republics except the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, was formed in late 1991 after the break-up of the Soviet Union.
But many parts of the defunct empire want to strengthen their independence rather than hand powers to the CIS.
A series of joint economic and political initiatives have come to nothing because smaller countries are reluctant to link themselves too closely to the Russia-dominated grouping.
Even Moscow officials have reservations about the CIS, and Russian news agencies quoted some Moscow officials who questioned the deal.
Interfax quoted Russian Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Davydov as saying the economic environment in the CIS has not been profitable for Moscow so far.

"There is no clear free trade zone or Most Favoured Nation system in the Commonwealth but rather a mixed-up indefinite system of trade relations drawn up for political reasons," said Davydov, who is also Foreign Trade minister.
"We had lived in a single state but later divorced," he added. "Under the new circumstances we should regulate trade relations so they do not harm Russia."
Davydov said Russia had suffered losses from a flow of poor quality cheap vodka imported from Ukraine through Belarus.
Russian officials have also complained that other CIS members do little to pay for energy supplies from Russia.
